extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, and news professionals (editors, producers, reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria that guide how news organizations (magazines and television) generate, sell, select, and shape story ideas from reporters and sources into finished news items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to suggest story ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters (and other staff) are formally assigned to find or think up story ideas and are evaluated in part by their ability to suggest suitable stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All staff, including top editors and nonjournalists, are expected to generate ideas; magazines often begin editorial meetings with informal reviews of social activities to produce story ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wire services as a story source
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services continuously spin out stories that serve as suggestions for follow-up by magazine or television reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire output provides a 24-hour stream of potential leads that story suggesters can convert into followups or fuller coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated (prescheduled) stories as a resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipated stories are preplanned events (news conferences, speeches, hearings, ceremonies) that provide predictable, accessible newsworthy material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipated stories assure availability and allow scheduling of crews; sources preschedule events knowing journalists' dependence on them; not all anticipated stories are suitable, but they form a large portion of coverage (e.g., two-thirds in one sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and producibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selectors check whether a suggested story "is actually available and feasible," i.e., whether it can be reported and produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories may be killed or postponed because needed information is unavailable, they require too much rewriting/editing, or they become stale or no longer newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / up-to-dateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for the most up-to-date material; newer stories can 'space out' older ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both selection and production are continuous processes; staying current is prioritized to keep broadcasts/magazines relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-related vs audience-related judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists nearer sources judge stories from sources' perspective, while top producers/editors judge from the audience perspective; the final story is often a compromise but usually more audience-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat reporters may identify with sources and emphasize technical advances, whereas editors will emphasize audience benefit or human interest (example: medical research framed for patient benefit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salability (what will sell to selectors/audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggesters identify and advertise the most salable elements of a story—novel, dramatic, or unusual components—to persuade selectors who cannot accept everything offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sellers combine salient advance information with knowledge of buyers' preferences but avoid false advertising; enthusiasm from the suggester helps persuade buyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting (selecting dramatic/distinctive elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers 'highlight' the most dramatic or distinctive parts of an event; highlighting is intrinsic to both selling and production and leads to a 'highlights of highlights' version of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting proceeds spirally across stages (reporters pick highlights, writers pick some of those); examples include TV reporters filming only dramatic portions of speeches and magazines selecting striking scenes from files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overselling (maintain credibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggesters must avoid overselling their ideas because overselling casts doubt on their credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because suggesters are judged partly on how often their ideas are chosen, they advertise their ideas but should not promise more than they can deliver; hard selling is risky when the suggester cannot deliver the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to independently corroborated interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Buyers pay more attention if several suggesters independently sell the same story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinated or multiple-sourced selling increases perceived salability and likelihood of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of 'running stories' and 'running actors'
rubrics_metrics.description: Installments of ongoing events (wars, elections, inflation) or recurring public figures (presidents) are pre-favored for coverage because they form continuing narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every installment makes the final list, but continuity and familiarity with actors make such items more likely to be selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on known public figures and conflict/disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: News tends to be dominated by well-known public officials and stories of conflict/disorder because those elements are easier to highlight and assume audience interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting and salability help explain this dominance; organizational practices further favor famous actors and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling to fit media workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources and event organizers time activities (e.g., hearings in the morning; key witnesses early) to match news media work schedules and camera availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing decisions are often strategic to ensure coverage; experienced organizers schedule demonstrations and events to fit camera crews' schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational hierarchy and final authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors and producers have final say in story selection and shape the final product; their preferences and decisions set tones and sometimes precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although decisions are hierarchical, consultation with reporters and section heads occurs; who holds final authority matters less than the shared considerations that define news judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive constraints: budgets and personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate and news executives influence story selection indirectly via budget and staffing decisions that affect news-gathering capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower budgets make coverage harder; new executives or top editors brought from outside can alter priorities; executives may intervene intermittently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive role in policy and 'touchy' content
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives set policy (often informally) for sensitive coverage (to minimize visibility in social disorders) and rule on stories raising commercial, political, or taste issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executives may rule on profanity, sacrilege, nudity, terrorism coverage, or high-profile editorial positions (e.g., endorsements), sometimes requiring consultation before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity pressures of production
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations produce conformity pressures—people must cooperate to meet deadlines; noncooperation (prima donnas, chronic objectors) leads to isolation or job loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conformity extends to work habits, lunches, office banter, values/ideology, and even dress; the assembly-line nature of newswork amplifies conformity demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation and variation in decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of delegation (who actually makes decisions) varies by organizational tradition and leader style and can create semi-autonomous units within magazines or networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in centralization (e.g., Newsweek vs Time) reflect personal styles and attempts to improve quality or morale; delegation level affects daily selection dynamics but not the underlying news criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual autonomy tied to seniority and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and reporters enjoy varying degrees of autonomy—star and senior writers are largely autonomous; juniors must earn autonomy through performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior editors generally set word allotments and make suggestions, but substantive judgments (facts, conclusions) are commonly left to writers unless the editor intervenes; too much protest or disagreement brands one a 'crank.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sellers shape content via staged selling process
rubrics_metrics.description: The selling process is multi-stage (source → reporter → bureau chief → section head → top editor) and at each stage the idea may be altered to emphasize elements attractive to later buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different parts of a story are reemphasized to appeal to subsequent decision-makers; the seller anticipates preferences of later buyers and alters the 'product' accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting can construct a new story (not just summarize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting sometimes ignores the observed event and constructs a new story by selecting elements that reframe or exaggerate reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a press conference with many speakers where coverage focuses on one newsworthy figure whose actual role was minor; the resulting piece centers that figure and dramatizes selected moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters' identification with sources can bias suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat reporters sometimes identify with their sources, which can lead selectors to discount or alter their story suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source-related reporting may emphasize technical or insider advances while audience-related editors will reframe for public interest; this tension influences which stories survive selection.
